title: The Atlas Computer and the Invention of Virtual Memory (1962)
explainer: The memory-management subsystem you design for a kernel rests on an idea first built at the University of Manchester: the Atlas computer, commissioned in December 1962 under Tom Kilburn, was the first machine to automatically page data between a small, fast core store and a larger, slower drum, giving programs the illusion of one large 'one-level store.' That mechanism is what later systems called virtual memory, and the page tables, page faults, and eviction policies you implement in a kernel subsystem are direct descendants of a scheme built specifically to work around real, expensive 1960s hardware.

title: Unix's Kernel Was Born on a Spare, Underpowered PDP-7 (1969)
explainer: Before Unix had a shell or a philosophy, its kernel existed because Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, and Rudd Canaday sketched a file-system design and implemented it in the summer of 1969 on a largely idle PDP-7 that other groups had passed over as too weak. That specific hardware shaped early kernel decisions directly, including the choice to treat I/O devices as files, and the whole system was rewritten again after Bell Labs funded a move to the more capable PDP-11. It's a concrete reminder that a kernel's subsystem boundaries often get negotiated with whatever hardware is actually on hand, not derived purely from first principles.
